name: Georgia
summary_text: Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it closes both routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.  The document problem predates the ban and is now absolute. Legal activists had been pressing for gender recognition reform for more than a decade on the grounds that official paperwork failing to match a person's identity made job applications difficult and exposed them to disclosure; from 2024 no recognition procedure is available at all, so a trans visitor's passport or ID will carry whatever marker their home jurisdiction issued, with no legal mechanism to alter it in Georgia and no lawful route to transition-related care if it is needed during the stay.  One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" measures, had raised fears of hate crimes in the country. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.  Assembly rights were already constrained before the statutory ban. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in its planned city-centre locations on safety grounds, while organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march and far-right groups vowed to thwart it. Public LGBT assembly has since been prohibited outright.  The domestic protection machinery has been formally found wanting. A report submitted on 5 August 2024 by WISG and partner organisations to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions calls for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

sources.documents: Documents discrimination/violence: 32% experienced physical violence, 89.93% psychological violence; 73% of physical-violence victims never reported to police due to ineffectiveness/fear of homophobic treatment.

name: Gibraltar
summary_text: Gibraltar stands under the United Kingdom framework with its own Parliament and Supreme Court which enact and interpret its civil and criminal law. United Kingdom legislation does not apply automatically in Gibraltar. The Secretary of State stated on 1 April 2010 that international obligations could be imposed by Order in Council.  No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker. The sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route.  The Equal Opportunities Act 2006 came into force on 1 March 2007 and prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on grounds including gender reassignment. The Act defines gender reassignment as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person’s sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. The same Act prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or both.  Male same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and the Government of the United Kingdom. No criminal prohibition relevant to same-sex conduct is recorded as remaining in force.  The Crimes Act 2011 was amended to criminalise hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation. Parliament approved the bill on 19 September 2013, royal assent was given on 25 September and the provision took effect on 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.  In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy.  Gibraltar provides recognition for same-sex partnerships. Parliament passed a civil partnership law in March 2014 granting same-sex couples most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling. The Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 was passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December 2016, with the first marriage the next day. Where a deputy registrar opts out of officiating a same-sex marriage, an alternative registrar must be assigned.
